description: "Add passwordless auth (passkeys, magic links, email and SMS one-time codes) to a Next.js App Router app without writing JWT, cookie, or refresh code: one install, one route handler, proxy.ts protection, and a complete sign-in component."

  order: 1.2

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

This page is for a Next.js App Router app that needs sign-in and is about to grow a hand-written
JWT helper in a route handler or `middleware.ts`. `@seamless-auth/nextjs` replaces that helper. One
catch-all route handler serves the `/auth` routes the browser SDK calls, the session lives in
signed `HttpOnly` cookies on your app's own origin, and `proxy.ts`, server components, and your
own route handlers read the session with one function call each. Sign-in itself (passkeys, magic
links, email and SMS one-time codes, OAuth) runs on a Seamless Auth server: self-hosted
[`seamless-auth-api`](/build/auth-api) or a managed instance. There is no separate API server.

**Why not write the 40 lines yourself?** Signing a token is the easy part. The work is everywhere
around it: where the token lives so a script cannot read it, refresh that rotates without logging
people out (a refresh during server rendering, whose response the browser never sees, is a classic
way to revoke your own users), revoking a stolen session, and the passkey (WebAuthn) ceremonies,
which no JWT helper covers. The adapter and the auth server do all of that, and the adapter's tests
hold it to the same responses as the Express adapter.

Versions on this page: `@seamless-auth/nextjs` 0.4.0, `@seamless-auth/react` 0.16.0, Next.js 16,
`seamless-cli` 0.22.0. All Seamless Auth packages are pre-1.0.

---

## Fastest Path: A New Project

One command, no prompts, safe for scripts and agents:

```bash
npx seamless-cli init my-app --nextjs --local --yes --email=you@example.com
cd my-app
docker compose up
```

`--nextjs` picks the full-stack Next.js starter (marked beta) in place of the React and Express
pair. The app runs on `http://localhost:5173` with the admin console at `/console`, and the auth
server runs in Docker. Register with the email you passed and that account becomes the first
admin. The [Self-Hosted Quickstart](/start/quickstart) walks through the same flow.

---

## Add It To An Existing Next.js App

<Aside type="note">
  [`seamless add`](/operate/add-to-existing-app), the CLI command that wires an existing project,
  does not support Next.js yet.
  The steps below are the whole integration.
</Aside>

### 1. Have An Auth Server

Create a managed application in the portal ([Managed Quickstart](/start/managed-quickstart)), or
run [`seamless-auth-api`](/build/auth-api) yourself. You need its URL and its service token. Add
your app's origin (for example `http://localhost:3000`) to the auth server's `ORIGINS`, or passkey
ceremonies fail.

### 2. Install

```bash
npm install @seamless-auth/nextjs @seamless-auth/react
```

`react-router-dom` is not needed. The examples import with `@/`, the alias `create-next-app` sets
up.

### 3. The Options, In One Place

```ts
// lib/seamless.ts
import type { SeamlessAuthHandlerOptions, SeamlessAuthMessagingOptions } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

// Development only: print one-time codes and magic links to the `next dev` output
// instead of sending them, so you can sign in with no mail or SMS provider.
const devMessaging: SeamlessAuthMessagingOptions = {
  handlers: {
    sendOtpEmail: async ({ to, token }) => {
      console.log(`Dev code for ${to}: ${token}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'email' }
    },
    sendOtpSms: async ({ to, token }) => {
      console.log(`Dev code for ${to}: ${token}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'sms' }
    },
    sendMagicLinkEmail: async ({ to, magicLinkUrl }) => {
      console.log(`Dev magic link for ${to}: ${magicLinkUrl}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'email' }
    },
  },
}

// A function, not a constant: `next build` imports route modules without your secrets.
export function seamlessOptions(): SeamlessAuthHandlerOptions {
  // Set AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER only when the auth server signs as a different URL from
  // the one this app calls, as the local Docker stack does (http://auth:5312).
  const issuer = process.env.AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER || undefined

  return {
    authServerUrl: process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
    authServerIssuer: issuer,
    audience: issuer ?? process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
    cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY!,
    serviceSecret: process.env.API_SERVICE_TOKEN!,
    jwksKid: process.env.JWKS_KID,
    messaging: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? undefined : devMessaging,
  }
}
```

### 4. Serve `/auth` From One Route Handler

```ts
// app/auth/[...seamless]/route.ts
import { createSeamlessAuthHandler, type SeamlessAuthRouteHandlers } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'
import { seamlessOptions } from '@/lib/seamless'

// Every route the browser SDK calls: passkeys, magic links, OTP, refresh, logout.
let handlers: SeamlessAuthRouteHandlers | undefined
const seamless = () => (handlers ??= createSeamlessAuthHandler(seamlessOptions()))

export const GET = (request: Request) => seamless().GET(request)
export const POST = (request: Request) => seamless().POST(request)
export const PUT = (request: Request) => seamless().PUT(request)
export const PATCH = (request: Request) => seamless().PATCH(request)
export const DELETE = (request: Request) => seamless().DELETE(request)
```

The handler is created on the first request, so `next build` passes without a `.env`. It needs the
Node.js runtime, which is the default; do not set `runtime = 'edge'`. Export all five methods:
`PUT` is new in 0.4.0.

### 5. Protect Pages In `proxy.ts`

```ts
// proxy.ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server'
import { hasSeamlessSession } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  if (hasSeamlessSession(request.cookies, { cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY! })) {
    return NextResponse.next()
  }

  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url))
}

export const config = { matcher: ['/dashboard/:path*'] }
```

The check is local, with no network call. A valid refresh cookie counts as signed in, because the
browser renews an expired access cookie on its next call to `/auth`. `proxy.ts` is the Next.js 16
name. On Next.js 15.5, name the file `middleware.ts`, export the function as `middleware`, and add
`runtime: 'nodejs'` to `config`: the Edge runtime cannot verify the cookies. If your app uses a
`src/` directory, the file goes in `src/`.

### 6. Protect Your Own API Routes And Read The User

```ts
// app/api/me/route.ts
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { getSeamlessClaims } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'

export async function GET() {
  const claims = getSeamlessClaims(await cookies(), {
    cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY!,
  })

  if (!claims) return Response.json({ error: 'unauthenticated' }, { status: 401 })

  return Response.json({ id: claims.id, roles: claims.roles })
}
```

`getSeamlessClaims` verifies the access cookie locally and returns `id`, `roles`, and usually
`email` and `phone`, or `null`. For a role check, `hasScopedRole(claims.roles, 'admin')`, also
exported from `@seamless-auth/nextjs`.

### 7. Add The Provider

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from 'react'
import { cookies, headers } from 'next/headers'
import { getSeamlessSession } from '@seamless-auth/nextjs'
import { AuthProvider } from '@seamless-auth/react'
import { seamlessOptions } from '@/lib/seamless'

export default async function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  // null is signed out. undefined (auth server unreachable) lets the provider find out in the browser.
  const session = await getSeamlessSession(await cookies(), {
    ...seamlessOptions(),
    userAgent: (await headers()).get('user-agent') ?? undefined,
  }).catch(() => undefined)

  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuthProvider apiHost="" initialSession={session}>
          {children}
        </AuthProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

`apiHost=""` sends every auth request to `/auth` on the page's own origin, the handler from step 4.
`initialSession` renders the signed-in user on the first paint. `getSeamlessSession` never
refreshes, by design: an expired access cookie returns `null` and the provider renews the session
in the browser straight after the page loads.

<Aside type="danger">
  Never call your own `/auth/users/me` from server code with the browser's cookies forwarded. When
  the access cookie has expired, the adapter refreshes inside that request, the browser never sees
  the new refresh token, and its next refresh is treated as a replay that revokes the session.
</Aside>

### 8. A Sign-In Page

`AuthRoutes`, the React SDK's built-in screens, route with react-router, so a Next.js app builds
its sign-in screen from the hooks. This component signs in with a passkey when the account has
one, falls back to an emailed code, and registers new accounts:

```tsx
// components/SignIn.tsx
'use client'

import { useState, type FormEvent } from 'react'
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
import { useAuth, useAuthClient, usePasskeySupport } from '@seamless-auth/react'

export default function SignIn() {
  const router = useRouter()
  const { login, handlePasskeyLogin, refreshSession } = useAuth()
  const client = useAuthClient()
  const { passkeySupported } = usePasskeySupport()

  const [mode, setMode] = useState<'login' | 'register'>('login')
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('')
  const [code, setCode] = useState('')
  const [codeSent, setCodeSent] = useState(false)
  const [error, setError] = useState('')

  async function finish() {
    await refreshSession()
    router.replace('/dashboard')
    router.refresh()
  }

  async function start(event: FormEvent) {
    event.preventDefault()
    setError('')

    if (mode === 'register') {
      const { error } = await client.register({ email })
      if (error) return setError('That account could not be created.')
      return setCodeSent(true)
    }

    const { data, error } = await login(email, passkeySupported)
    if (error) return setError('Sign-in could not start.')

    // Passkey first when the account has one; otherwise fall back to an emailed code.
    if (passkeySupported && data.loginMethods?.includes('passkey')) {
      const { error } = await handlePasskeyLogin()
      if (!error) return finish()
    }

    const { error: sendError } = await client.requestLoginEmailOtp()
    if (sendError) return setError('The code could not be sent.')
    setCodeSent(true)
  }

  async function verify(event: FormEvent) {
    event.preventDefault()
    const { error } =
      mode === 'register'
        ? await client.verifyEmailOtp(code)
        : await client.verifyLoginEmailOtp(code)

    if (error) {
      return setError(error.status === 429 ? 'Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes.' : 'That code did not match.')
    }
    await finish()
  }

  return codeSent ? (
    <form onSubmit={verify}>
      <label>
        The six-letter code we emailed you
        <input value={code} onChange={(e) => setCode(e.target.value.trim())} autoComplete="one-time-code" />
      </label>
      <button type="submit">Verify</button>
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
    </form>
  ) : (
    <form onSubmit={start}>
      <label>
        Email
        <input type="email" value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} autoComplete="username webauthn" />
      </label>
      <button type="submit">{mode === 'login' ? 'Sign in' : 'Create account'}</button>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => setMode(mode === 'login' ? 'register' : 'login')}>
        {mode === 'login' ? 'New here? Create an account' : 'Have an account? Sign in'}
      </button>
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
    </form>
  )
}
```

```tsx
// app/login/page.tsx
import SignIn from '@/components/SignIn'

export default function LoginPage() {
  return <SignIn />
}
```

Any client component reads the user with `useAuth()` (`user`, `isAuthenticated`, `logout`) and
calls your own routes with `useAuthorizedFetch()`. Emailed codes are six letters, not digits. For
magic links, SMS codes, and enrolling a passkey after registration, see
[How To Build Your Own Auth UI](/build/custom-auth-ui); the Next.js starter's
`src/components/SignIn.tsx` implements all of them.

### 9. Environment Variables

For an app run on the host against the local Docker stack:

```bash
# .env.local
AUTH_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:5312
AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER=http://auth:5312
API_SERVICE_TOKEN=the-auth-servers-API_SERVICE_TOKEN
COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY=output-of-openssl-rand-base64-48
JWKS_KID=dev-main
```

| Variable             | What it is                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AUTH_SERVER_URL`    | The Seamless Auth server this app calls. For a managed application, the Auth Server URL from the portal                                                       |
| `AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER` | Only for an app run on the host against the local Docker stack, which signs as `http://auth:5312`. Leave it unset otherwise                                    |
| `API_SERVICE_TOKEN`  | The secret shared with the auth server, 32 characters or more. Locally, the auth server's `API_SERVICE_TOKEN`; managed, a service token generated in the portal |
| `COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY` | Signs the session cookies, 32 characters or more. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 48`                                                                  |
| `JWKS_KID`           | Key id on the service tokens the adapter signs. The local stack uses `dev-main`; the adapter warns while it is `dev-main`, so set your own in production      |

None of these is `NEXT_PUBLIC_`: they stay on the server. The handler checks both secrets on the
first request.

---

## What Not To Write Yourself

With the route handler mounted, delete or never write:

- JWT signing or verification with `jose` or `jsonwebtoken` in `middleware.ts` or route handlers
- a `/api/login`, `/api/logout`, `/api/refresh`, or `/api/me` route for the session itself
- code that sets or clears auth cookies, or stores tokens in `localStorage`
- refresh-token rotation, reuse detection, or session revocation
- a server-side refresh during rendering (see the warning in step 7)
- password hashing, reset emails, or a passwords column
- WebAuthn challenge and attestation handling for passkeys
- one-time code or magic link generation, expiry, and rate limiting
